questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling price and a rising duty on the same households
questions.learningObjective: link a terms-of-trade movement to rural indebtedness
questions.stem: For two decades an export price falls steadily while the duty on imported goods is raised, and through the same period a growing share of small holdings appears in the mortgage registers. Which sequence best links the two movements?

options.text: A falling price cuts the income that can service a loan, while the higher duty raises the cost of leaving production
The mortgages caused the price to fall, since fewer goods were being sent abroad
options.misconception: inverts the causal order between a credit system and an export price

options.text: The price fell because of the mortgages, and the duties were then lowered to match it
options.misconception: both reverses the order and contradicts the direction of the duty change

options.text: The two movements are unconnected, since inland credit is independent of world markets
options.misconception: assumes inland credit cannot respond to an export price

questions.learningObjective: identify which administrative arrangement carried the most load after partition
questions.stem: After a border divides a region, customs posts stand along it, the railway line is rerouted to serve each side's new capital, two currencies are issued, and an outside commission is appointed to hold posts and fund ministries until local officials are trained. An outside commission was needed, so the new state had no prospect of staffing its own service
options.misconception: converts a temporary arrangement into a permanent incapacity

options.text: Two currencies were issued, so the border had already become permanent in the ordinary sense
options.misconception: reads an administrative necessity as proof of a settled frontier

options.text: The railway was rerouted, so the line to a capital decided which province belonged where
options.misconception: makes a transport consequence the cause of the territorial division

The distractors each mistake a temporary arrangement for a permanent incapacity, a proof of permanence, or the cause of the division itself.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the arrangement the new government could not yet do for itself.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colony financed from the capital
questions.learningObjective: analyse how dependent financing relocates priority setting
questions.stem: A modern summary of a colony's annual financial statement records that the greater part of its receipts is a grant from the metropolitan treasury, that no new tax may be levied without approval from the capital, and that each year's works and schools are paid for within the grant's stated conditions. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

options.text: That taxation and spending are decided in the capital, so the colony's budget runs on conditions
That the colony was well run, since its revenue came from a dependable source
options.misconception: reads a funding arrangement as an assessment of administration

options.text: That the local administration had asked for a larger grant and been refused it
options.misconception: infers a request and a refusal the statement does not record

options.text: That the grant was made once and was never varied afterwards
options.misconception: asserts a permanence the annual renewal of a grant contradicts

questions.explanation: The three entries in the statement point the same way, since money that arrives from elsewhere, a prohibition on raising more without leave, and spending limited to what the grant's conditions allow, each place the decision about priorities in the capital rather than in the colony. That is a statement about where authority over the budget sits, and it is a different claim from a judgement about whether the arrangement served the colony well, which the summary does not address. Each distractor supplies a verdict on administration, an unrecorded refusal, or a permanence that an annual statement cannot establish.
questions.hint: Ask where each year's spending decision is actually made, and by whom.

questions.topic: Two campaigns with the same equipment

options.misconception: invents a force comparison the record does not supply

options.text: The first advance was carried by troops the second campaign did not have available
options.misconception: supposes a difference in troops between two campaigns of one force

A single dependency, since the company's purchases decided the government's revenue

questions.learningObjective: analyse how war measures raise costs inside the belligerent's own economy

options.misconception: assigns a self-inflicted effect to the other belligerent's action

options.text: Rising food prices show the harvest failed, since a levy of labour cannot affect the price of bread

Disputes involving foreign nationals begin to be heard by their own consuls instead of the local courts

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a monopoly can inform a buyer and still charge more
questions.learningObjective: explain how removing sellers can improve information while worsening terms
questions.stem: Explain how a market with a single seller can leave a buyer better informed than a market with many sellers, and why that improvement can arrive together with worse terms for the buyer.

answer.exemplar: A buyer with many sellers learns from the sellers themselves, since the offers differ in quality, in credit terms and in price, and a difference between two offers is a comparison the buyer can use. Remove the other sellers and the comparison goes, but so does the need to keep improving terms, because the remaining seller knows that a buyer who has nowhere else to go will not walk away over a small difference, which is the same fact from the two sides. The two facts are compatible, and the case where they diverge is the one worth naming: a monopoly can still reduce cost. A sole supplier with a fleet of its own can charge a higher freight rate and still deliver more cheaply than carriers who must buy fuel at the market price, and a buyer is better off even though the price has gone up. So the question is not whether a monopoly improves matters but which matter it is spending its advantage on. The gain in information comes from the last seller having a reason to publish, since a buyer who knows nothing can be sold anything, and a seller who wants repeat custom has to say what the goods actually are; the loss in terms comes from the buyer having nothing to compare that with. The practical consequence is that a market with one seller can be honest about its goods and still uncompetitive about its price, which is why a monopoly that is required to publish and one that is required to sell cheaply are quite different arrangements and are routinely confused.

The two facts are compatible, and the case where they diverge is the one worth naming: a monopoly can still reduce cost. A sole supplier with a fleet of its own can charge a higher freight rate and still deliver more cheaply than carriers who must buy fuel at the market price, and a buyer is better off even though the price has gone up. So the question is not whether a monopoly improves matters but which matter it is spending its advantage on. The gain in information comes from the last seller having a reason to publish, since a buyer who knows nothing can be sold anything, and a seller who wants repeat custom has to say what the goods actually are; the loss in terms comes from the buyer having nothing to compare that with. The practical consequence is that a market with one seller can be honest about its goods and still uncompetitive about its price, which is why a monopoly that is required to publish and one that is required to sell cheaply are quite different arrangements and are routinely confused.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A line that is certain and contested at once
questions.learningObjective: explain how legal certainty and practical dispute can coexist on one frontier
questions.stem: Explain how a frontier could be completely settled as a matter of law and still be disputed on the ground, and name the step that produced each state of affairs.

answer.exemplar: The two states are produced by two different acts. A commission walks the ground, chooses points, marks them, and writes a schedule of what lies on each side, and the two governments accept that text, and from that moment the frontier is certain in the only sense that matters to a court, a customs officer or a land office, because there is a document that says where the line runs and no one who must apply it has any discretion left. Certainty of that kind is entirely compatible with dispute on the ground, because the schedule cannot describe what people actually do: a grazing route that crossed the line, a well on the wrong side of it, a village whose fields it divided, an official marker moved or washed away. Those are not contradictions of the text, they are the ordinary consequence of drawing a line through a lived landscape, and they recur because the line is a description of a boundary rather than a correction of one. The step that produced certainty was the survey being accepted in a signed instrument; the step that produced the disputes was the same survey, since a survey must choose points where the land offers none and must convert a region of use into a sequence of assigned villages. Anyone hoping to explain such a frontier by reading the treaty alone will find nothing contested in it, and anyone hoping to explain it by looking at the ground will find no line at all, and the reconciliation is that the two were never describing the same object.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a local crisis reaches the size of a general war
questions.learningObjective: explain how conditional commitments multiply a local dispute
questions.stem: Explain how a dispute confined to one frontier became a war between several great powers, and name the two features of the alliance system that made the multiplication possible.

answer.exemplar: Two features do the work, and the first is that the promises were conditional rather than automatic. A treaty that says an attack on one member is an attack on all of us is simple to extend, and it obliges nobody until something is judged to have happened, which puts a question of interpretation in the path of every obligation. A power deciding whether to move must first decide whether the attack counts, who caused it, and whether the moment of striking was chosen by the other side, and each of those judgements is a place where a government can hesitate, and hesitation is what later is read as consent by the other side. The second feature is that the promises were mutual in the sense that mattered for fear: a power that is protected is a power that does not need allies as urgently, and so the protection is undermined by the appearance of weakness, which converts a defensive arrangement into a standing incentive to act first rather than to deliberate. Add to those two features the ordinary mechanics of a great power's mobilisation, which takes days and must therefore be announced and timed, and the multiplication is easy to trace. A local dispute produces a report; the report is written in a vocabulary that names it an attack; a note is sent whose deadline is set at the point where mobilisation can begin; the reply rejects the note; allies read their treaties and find that the wording covers what has been described; and several states begin moving trains on timetables that were already drawn for a different reason. Each step is defensible on its own terms, and that is the difficulty: no single government has to choose a general war, only to answer for the step in front of it, while the step in front of it was made necessary by someone else's step. The clearest account of a general war is therefore not a list of grievances but a sequence of conditional obligations, each of which was satisfied by an interpretation, and it is worth adding that the same structure would have produced a negotiated settlement if any one interpretation had been disputed slowly enough for someone to lose interest in the deadline.
